source.title: Early Stopping Against Label Noise Without Validation Data
source.authors: Su-Qin Yuan; Lei Feng; Tongliang Liu

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. It identifies itself as published at ICLR 2024, although the supplied arXiv identifier is from 2025.
record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own results and qualifications about generalization with noisy labels, including when its early-stopping method works and when it does not. Its main focus is early stopping under label noise, rather than the claim versions’ specific standard-training tests.
record.gate_note: The paper studies early stopping with noisy labels. It does not test memorization of random labels, natural-label generalization under the same recipes, or the listed architecture, optimizer, batch-size, dropout, sharpness, and memorized-example interventions as framed by V1–V8. Its training-error, test-error, and prediction-change trajectories under label noise are relevant to the broader claim that fitting and generalization can diverge, but do not directly measure the specific behaviors in those versions.
record.test_reason: Appendix C.5, Table 5 tests V6 in a noisy-label setting: adding dropout improves CIFAR-10 test accuracy with batch normalization and data augmentation, both with and without mixup. The record overlooks these controlled comparisons.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: the authors conclude that training-set prediction changes enable early stopping without separate validation data in many noisy-label settings and can improve existing noisy-label methods. They also identify a transitional learning-confusion stage and acknowledge that Label Wave may fail with very low or no noise or when that stage is absent.
record.recipe_differences: Studies early stopping in noisy-label learning using training-set prediction changes, rather than the claim versions’ interventions or measurements. Tests noisy labels and model-selection performance.
record.method_sensitivity: The authors report that Label Wave may not work with very low or no label noise, or when training lacks a learning-confusion stage. Performance is evaluated across datasets, architectures, batch sizes, learning rates, optimizers, noise types, and noise rates.

fits_no_version.finding: During noisy-label training, increasing fit to mislabeled examples coincides with rising test error and reduced prediction stability on clean training examples.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Fitting noisy labels can impair generalization and stable fitting of clean examples during a transitional training stage.

fits_no_version.finding: Prediction-change-based early stopping selects near-best checkpoints across many noisy-label settings, but may fail without a learning-confusion stage.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Training prediction changes can guide early stopping under label noise when a learning-confusion stage occurs.

record.problems: The central test-error and prediction-fluctuation trajectories are shown in figures without numeric values in the supplied text. The paper notes that Label Wave may fail with low or no noise and where the learning-confusion stage is absent. No numeric results directly test V1–V8.
record.rows_left_out: No qualifying result rows for V1–V8. Reported Label Wave-versus-global-maximum and Label Wave-versus-validation accuracy results evaluate the proposed model-selection method, not the specific behaviors named in the versions; the paper’s own method comparison is excluded by the row rules.

untested.parts: No paired random-label memorization and natural-label generalization experiment.
No width sweep beyond the width needed to interpolate.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison on the same image task.
Optimizer variations evaluate early-stopping selection; no controlled comparison establishing the claimed generalization difference under limited tuning.
No established fixed-epoch comparison of large-batch penalties or recipe adaptations.
No very-small-training-set experiment, dropout-strength sweep, or joint removal of dropout and weight decay. The dropout configuration is unspecified.
No magnitude-aware sharpness measurements or comparison with norm- and margin-based measures.
No removal of examples selected by memorization influence followed by retraining.

missing.what: Dropout ablation without mixup: record test accuracy with versus without dropout separately for Label Wave selection (83.57±0.24% versus 81.61±0.44%) and 20% hold-out validation selection (81.30±1.07% versus 78.94±0.52%). Both configurations include batch normalization and data augmentation.
missing.locator: Appendix C.5, Table 5, rows Label Wave + BN + DA and Label Wave + BN + DA + Dropout.

missing.what: Dropout ablation with mixup: record test accuracy with versus without dropout separately for Label Wave selection (83.67±0.45% versus 82.38±0.56%) and 20% hold-out validation selection (81.66±0.07% versus 81.06±0.49%). Both configurations include batch normalization and data augmentation.
missing.locator: Appendix C.5, Table 5, rows Label Wave + BN + DA + Mixup and Label Wave + BN + DA + Dropout + Mixup.

record.verdict_notes: The empty row set and assertion that no results test V1–V8 require correction. Table 5 contains dropout ablations, not merely comparisons of model-selection methods. The verdicts use matched selection procedures and do not rely on the oracle global-maximum column.

versions.untested_parts: Does not compare random-label memorization with natural-label generalization under the same recipes.
No convolutional versus fully connected comparison.
Does not compare adaptive optimizers and SGD on generalization; optimizers are varied only to assess Label Wave selection.
Does not test large-batch generalization penalties under fixed epoch budgets.
Does not test dropout’s effect on held-out error as framed by this version; dropout appears among Label Wave configurations.
Does not remove memorized examples and retrain.

relationships.condition: CIFAR-10 with 40% symmetric label noise, batch normalization and data augmentation, without mixup.
relationships.reason: Table 5 reports accuracy rising from 81.61±0.44% to 83.57±0.24% with dropout under Label Wave selection; validation selection also improves, from 78.94±0.52% to 81.30±1.07%. Based on text; corresponding rows are missing.
relationships.display_finding: Dropout reportedly improved accuracy under both selection methods without mixup, but these comparisons remain unverified.
